Amazon.com Investment Narrative Recap

For an investor to stay with Amazon.com, the core belief is that heavy AWS and AI infrastructure spending eventually converts strong operating income into sustained free cash flow. According to rcb9, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the real story is operating profit of US$27.5b rather than the Anthropic driven net income headline. The key near term catalyst is whether AWS demand and backlog keep supporting that 39% margin while depreciation from US$220b of annual capex builds.

The largest risk right now is that cash burn and rising debt persist if usage or backlog growth slow, which could leave trailing free cash flow weak even as reported earnings look healthy. Recent news around Amazon Autos expansion and the Decart AI talks does not yet change that core equation. Investors are still watching 2026 and early 2027 updates for direction on free cash flow, capex guidance and AWS growth.

The reported agreement to acquire Decart AI looks most relevant here because it ties straight into AWS economics. Management is already leaning on Amazon designed chips such as Trainium, and Decart's optimization tools are intended to cut compute costs for generative media workloads. If that integration works operationally, it can support the thesis that large AI capex is demand led, not just speculative capacity.

This move also interacts directly with the main catalyst and main risk rcb9 highlights. Better chip level efficiency can help protect AWS margins as depreciation from US$220b of annual spending flows through the income statement. At the same time, folding another AI asset into the stack adds execution complexity. Investors will likely track whether future AWS disclosure links Decart technology to measurable savings or usage trends rather than just one off headlines.

Tech stocks aren't lacking in growth stories for 2027. The problem is that smart money is increasingly selective about which companies it's willing to pay a premium for. AI is still the big story, but skepticism is growing about whether the money invested will deliver the promised returns.

You could see that shift very clearly in the Bank of America fund manager survey for November. Investors were clearly pulling back from tech at the fastest rate since June 2006 (their net overweight position in tech fell from 37% in October to just 12%). Even more telling is that 38% of the 169 managers surveyed (who in total manage $461 billion) believe that firms are over-investing in AI and over half (52%) expect at least one of the major AI players to reduce its capital expenditure over the next 6 months.

The concerns led to a wider sell-off. The Nasdaq 100 Index is down over 10% in the second half of 2026. Semiconductors were particularly hard hit as investors have re-priced AI companies and rethought the sustainability of data center spending. This wasn't necessarily a rejection of AI per se. It was more a case of investors questioning how much expected growth had already been priced in.

There's still a lot of money flowing into the sector. JPMorgan expects AI-related capex to be $1.4tn in 2027, almost double its 2026 estimate. A significant portion will go into data centers, servers, networking gear and advanced semiconductors. For a closer look at where this spending is going, see our breakdown of the eight companies Morgan Stanley expects to spend $1.6 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027. JPMorgan does, however, expect spending growth to tail off significantly from 2028.

The wider tech sector isn't moving in the same direction. Chip and data center suppliers are clearly on the up because of AI spending. On the other hand, the software and cloud businesses have to prove that their customers are actually going to spend more. For investors, it's all about separating the wheat from the chaff. Some businesses have sustainable demand while others are just in the midst of a spending spike.

title: Jeff Bezos makes a $200 million move involving Amazon stock
detail:
Jeff Bezos makes a $200 million move involving Amazon stock
Damilola Esebame, Celine Provini
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 11:03 AM PST 5 min read
AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When a company founder transfers shares valued at nearly $200 million in a week, most investors start looking for signs of trouble. 

Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings showed that Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos transferred 771,492 shares on Nov. 12 and 13, 2026.

The batch was valued at approximately $198.9 million based on Amazon's Nov. 16 closing price of $257.75, according to Nasdaq. 

This transfer, however, had nothing to do with Bezos exiting his position or signaling concern about the company he founded more than three decades ago.

Also Read: How Jeff Bezos added $102 billion to his fortune in one month

Bezos directed shares to nonprofits, not to the open market

Bezos transferred 674,088 shares on Nov. 12 and another 97,404 on the following day, the SEC filing disclosed on Nov. 16. The Bezos Earth Fund received the second, smaller batch worth approximately $25.1 million, a Form 144 SEC filing confirmed.

The foundation planned to sell those shares through Morgan Stanley after receiving them as a charitable gift from Bezos on Nov. 13. The remaining shares from the larger Nov. 12 transfer went to other nonprofit organizations not named in the public filings.

Bezos originally acquired these shares on July 5, 1994, the date he incorporated the company that would eventually become Amazon.

That was nearly three years before Amazon's 1997 initial public offering, which means those shares have appreciated from a near-zero cost basis to current prices.

Because these shares were donated, they never entered the open market, and no outside buyer was involved in the transfer. 

The transaction transferred ownership directly from Bezos to the charitable organizations, with Morgan Stanley handling the subsequent sale only on behalf of the Earth Fund.

Amazon's executive chairman has donated more than $629 million in shares this year

Bezos has followed this pattern throughout 2026, donating more than 1,253,797 shares in May and another 415,580 shares in late August. 

Those earlier batches, combined with the November transfers, bring total 2026 charitable giving to at least 2.44 million donated shares valued at roughly $629 million.

November has been tough on tech stocks. The Nasdaq Composite slid around 7% from the end of October to Wednesday, Nov. 25, putting the index about 15% below the record close it set on Oct. 6.

Some big growth stocks are down far more. Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) shares, at $59.41 after Wednesday's close, have lost over half their value since their record close in June 2025. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) trades around 14% under its Aug. 3 record close, and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) is about 22% off the record close it set on Oct. 9.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But I think all three are worth considering in December and holding into 2027. Each reported something in its last quarter that its stock price doesn't seem to reflect.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Netflix's members are staying put

Netflix raised prices again this year, including in the U.S. Still, its churn (the share of members who cancel) improved year over year in the third quarter, both worldwide and in the U.S. It was also better than management had predicted.

On the third-quarter earnings call in October, co-CEO Greg Peters called churn "the best evidence that we've got that we're delivering [value to members]."

This matters because much of Netflix's growth comes from raising prices, which tends to work only when members stay. And at around 16 times its expected 2027 earnings, Netflix is the cheapest of the three stocks.

But revenue growth might keep slowing. Third-quarter revenue climbed 11.8%, versus 17.2% growth a year before. And Netflix expects 11.5% for the fourth quarter. If growth keeps falling, the shares might stay cheap for a long time.

2. Amazon: chips it designs itself

Amazon Web Services (AWS), the company's cloud computing unit, grew revenue 39% year over year in the third quarter, its sixth straight quarter of faster growth. One part of AWS is growing even faster: the chips Amazon designs itself.

On the third-quarter earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy said the chips business is growing at "triple digit percentages year over year." He added that revenue commitments for Graviton, Amazon's general-purpose processor, and Trainium, its artificial intelligence (AI) chip, have each risen more than 20-fold in the last year. Customers using Amazon's own chips saved more than $2 billion in the third quarter alone, he said, and Amazon plans to offer Trainium outside AWS in late 2027. On Nov. 23, Amazon also agreed to buy Decart's AI optimization technology and hire the start-up's founders and engineers, who have worked with Amazon on Trainium since 2025.

title: Does Amazon's Profit Hang On One Business?
detail:
Does Amazon's Profit Hang On One Business?
Trefis Team
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 9:31 AM PST 4 min read
AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Anthropic Broke Its $83 IPO Price. What Did Facebook Do Next?

Most of Amazon.com's profit now comes from one business, its cloud unit, Amazon Web Services. In the quarter that ended in September, the cloud unit earned $17.8 billion of the company's $28.1 billion operating income. It did that on $46 billion of the $202 billion in revenue. That matters because the cloud is also where most of Amazon's heavy spending goes. So how did one unit come to carry so much?

Why is Amazon's cloud unit earning so much?

Sales at the cloud unit grew 39.3% from a year earlier. Management said that was the sixth straight quarter of faster growth, driven by both its core services and AI. The unit kept 38.7% of its sales as operating profit. Management put that down to strong growth and steady work on costs, including its own chips.

The store businesses earn far less on each dollar of sales. North America had an operating margin of 7.7% and International 3.7% in the same quarter. Their growth in the September quarter was also held down, because Prime Day moved into the June quarter. Management said growth in the quarter would have been about four percentage points higher without that shift.

Amazon's cloud unit keeps 38.7% of its sales as operating profit, against 7.7% for its North American stores. So the profit behind your Amazon shares leans on one unit, and the shares send you no regular cash to live on. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

How does Amazon's profit compare with its own past?

Amazon's operating margin over the twelve months to September was 13.1%. That is the highest twelve-month figure at any of the 40 quarter ends going back to December 2016. The margin was 9.8% in the twelve months to September 2024 and 2.6% in the twelve months to September 2022. So the company's profit sits at a ten-year high, and the cloud unit supplies most of it.

What could squeeze the cloud unit's margin?

The company does not forecast the cloud unit's margin. Management expects that margin to move with how much it is investing at the time. It also said the fast growth of AI weighs on the margin, because AI work earns less.

The investment is large. Amazon expects about $220 billion of cash capital spending in 2026, mostly for the cloud unit. It expects to spend meaningfully more in 2027. Over the twelve months to September, its free cash flow was minus $46.9 billion. In other words, the business spent more than it brought in, and the cloud's margin is what has to make that spending pay.
